newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia dollar-denominated MinFin bonds set records.
newsitem.headline: Russia dollar-denominated MinFin bonds set records.

text.p: Dollar-denominated Russian Ministry of Finance bonds, which for months have risen on investor confidence in Russia, set new records on Monday, tracking the U.S. Treasuries with which they are compared.

The price of the benchmark fourth tranche MinFin, as the bonds are known, which matures in 2003, rose 0.3 percentage points to yield 10.39 percent. The third tranche maturing in 1999 yielded a spare 8.70 percent.

The bonds, with daily turnover of up to several million dollars -- making them a contender for Russia's second biggest market after rouble-denominated T-bills -- have been tracking U.S. Treasuries which are also seeing prices rise strongly.
But with fears of U.S. inflation growing and perception of Russian risk decreasing, MinFins could outperform the U.S. paper.

"Generally, MinFins are looking quite attractive," said ICFI Moscow Partners Bank dealer Denis Sysoyev. "If there is a dip in MinFins in line with U.S. Treasuries, there should be somebody to buy MinFins on the back of positive news from Russia."

Russia issued the bonds domestically and abroad beginning in 1993 in order to pay Russian exporters hard currency it had borrowed. The total nominal outstanding value of the bonds, tranches 3 to 7, is $11 billion.
Salomon Brothers economy and market analyst David Boren said fears of U.S. inflation could narrow the gap between MinFins and U.S. Treasuries.
But investors may move out of MinFins into other higher yielding debt, he said.
"When you get to these levels, more investors are going to be comparing the kind of return on other Russian assets which are increasingly available," Boren added.
Russian dollar-denominated Vnesh loans, based on debts owed by the Former Soviet Union, trade at about 550 basis points over U.S. treasuries, against 425-450 for MinFins.
But MinFins, which are held and cleared in Russia, trade much higher than Russia's Eurobond which trades 250 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.

But Russia-related factors, such as negotiations on restructuring Russia's foreign debt, which was of major importance to the market some two years ago, are no longer the top issue on investors' lists, dealers said.
"We still are able to see MinFins some figures higher over next few months," said ICFI's Sysoyev said. "But in the short-term, they will be fluctuating with Treasuries."
Investors have become less concerned with criminal investigations which have dogged some MinFin issues, he said.

Russian authorities froze about $85 million in MinFins during criminal investigations last year and this year but dealers say the market, which has not seen new bonds frozen for months, was not overly concerned with the issue.
"Frozen MinFins has become a minor issue,"a Moscow Narodny Bank dealer said. "It is a concern for non-market professionals, the market itself is relaxed."
Investors hungry for Russian debt may be forced to the large MinFin market, he said.
Russia's Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov said on Monday Russia may not issue another Eurobond in 1997 as tax collection is rising.
"The news that Russia is unlikely to issue more Eurobonds this year can imply that more money will be flowing into other Russian papers," the dealer said.
